source.title: Nonasymptotic theory for two-layer neural networks: Beyond the bias-variance trade-off

record.file_problem: Full paper and supplementary material supplied; text is readable, though some equations and symbols show extraction artifacts.
record.tranche_reason: Provides a theoretical analysis of how width affects prediction error in two-layer ReLU networks, including a double-descent risk curve. It does not reproduce the empirical natural-label/random-label experiments in V1 or the width sweep in V2; the method and measure are theoretical risk bounds under explicit regularization.
record.gate_note: The paper gives theoretical bounds and a schematic risk curve, not measured training and test errors from experiments. Its numerical example is a plot derived from the prediction bound. Cited empirical findings, including fitting random labels while generalizing on natural labels, are not results of this paper.
record.test_reason: The study derives prediction-error upper bounds for explicitly regularized ReLU regression estimators. A decreasing upper bound does not establish that actual held-out error decreases with width. It neither identifies a zero-training-error threshold nor analyzes the unregularized classification behavior in V2. Its double-descent curve plots the bound, rather than measured or exactly characterized risk.
record.authors_conclusion: The paraphrase captures the authors' interpretation, but should specify that their results are bounds: they argue that width-dependent prediction bounds explain double descent for explicitly regularized two-layer ReLU regression. The bound's second valley can be lower in finite samples under equation (16), and its rate is nearly minimax optimal over their larger function class. They provide no empirical validation or proof that actual risk follows the plotted bound.
record.recipe_differences: The paper develops nonasymptotic theory for a penalized empirical-risk minimizer with explicit scaled variation regularization, rather than empirically training unregularized networks to fit labels.
record.method_sensitivity: The risk behavior depends on network width and, for the relative height of the two valleys, the signal-to-noise condition in equation (16).

fits_no_version.finding: The regularized regression prediction bound combines decreasing approximation error with an estimation term that eventually becomes independent of width. Its plotted curve has two valleys whose relative heights depend on signal strength, dimension, and sample size.
fits_no_version.proposed_claim: For globally optimized, scaled-variation-regularized two-layer ReLU regression estimators under C1–C3, prediction-error upper bounds can exhibit double descent as width varies.

fits_no_version.finding: Optimally tuned ridge estimators with fixed random features have a worst-case prediction-risk lower bound of CM/[d min(m,n)^(1/d)] over GM.
fits_no_version.proposed_claim: Fixed random feature regression can suffer dimensionality-dependent worst-case limitations over the studied target function class.

record.problems: The claim-relevant width findings are theoretical bounds under explicit regularization, not measured train/test error. The paper states bounds up to constants and presents the risk curve as an implication of those bounds; it does not empirically validate the specified benchmark settings.
record.rows_left_out: R4 is included as a comparator because it supplies a theoretical lower bound for random feature models, but it does not directly test a listed version. No other own measured results bear on the listed versions; empirical findings in the introduction and cited literature are prior work.

untested.parts: No own natural-label versus random-label fitting and held-out-accuracy comparison.
Actual test-error improvement beyond the width required for zero training error; unregularized training to convergence on MNIST or downsampled CIFAR-10.
Convolutional versus fully connected image classifiers and the contribution of local connectivity.
Adaptive optimizers versus SGD under specified tuning budgets.
Batch-size effects under fixed epoch budgets and adapted training recipes.
Dropout effects on held-out classification error.
Magnitude-aware sharpness and its correlation with generalization gaps.
Accuracy after removing memorized versus randomly selected training examples.

record.verdict_notes: Neither the conditional ordering of the bound's valleys nor its asymptotic rates warrant a limits_scope verdict on V2. Figure 1 is calculated from the prediction bound. Its caption states signal-to-noise ratio 1, whereas the p. 14 discussion states κ = 1 for the example; these are inconsistent under the paper's definition of κ.

versions.untested_parts: No experiment fits random labels or compares held-out accuracy on natural and random labels.

It analyzes width-dependent prediction risk theoretically for regularized two-layer ReLU networks under a nonparametric regression model. It does not test the specified MNIST or downsampled CIFAR-10 settings, unregularized training, or an empirical zero-training-error threshold.
No convolutional versus fully connected comparison.
No comparison of adaptive optimizers with SGD.

rows.note: The stated result is a theoretical upper bound, not an empirically measured error. The accompanying discussion says the approximation term decreases with m and the estimation term saturates beyond a threshold.
rows.check: Theorem 5 bounds prediction error; it does not establish monotonic improvement in actual error beyond interpolation. The estimator uses explicit regularization and a global optimum. Theorem 5's displayed bound is unnumbered on p. 13; equation (15) belongs to Theorem 3. The constant C multiplies the entire sum.

rows.subject: regularized two-layer ReLU network estimator
rows.size_stated: width m; minima at m0 ≍ (n/(d log n))d/(2d+3) and m1 ≍ √(n/(d log n))
rows.stage_stated: regularized empirical risk minimizer; global minimizer
rows.operation_detail: The paper compares the underparametrized and overparametrized minima of the theoretical risk curve and states a signal-to-noise condition under which the second valley is lower.

conditions.value: κ > (1/(d log n))((d log n/n)^(3/(2d))) as expressed in equation (16)

rows.measure: relative heights of first and second risk valleys
rows.baseline: first valley is O((d log n/n)(d+3)/(2d+3))
rows.value: second valley is O(√(d log n/n)); it can be lower than the first when condition (16) holds
rows.locator: Introduction and discussion following Theorem 5, equation (16), pp. 3, 14
rows.note: The second valley is not always lower; asymptotically its stated rate is slightly worse, and finite-sample ordering depends on the signal condition.
rows.check: The valleys describe the prediction bound, not established minima of actual risk. The recorded signal condition is incorrect: equation (16) defines κ = ||f*||_S²/(σ_ε² + ||f*||_S²) and requires κ > (1/2)^((2d+3)/d) (n/(d log n))^(3/(2d)). Also, m1 ≍ sqrt(n/(d log n)) is the bound's estimation-term saturation point; the second valley extends toward infinite width.

rows.stage_stated: ridge estimator with optimally tuned λ
rows.operation_detail: Proposition 5 gives a worst-case prediction-risk lower bound for random feature models as a comparator to fully trained two-layer networks.

conditions.value: Conditions (C2) and (C3); target functions in GM

rows.note: This is a lower bound for a different model family, not a result measuring the width effect in V2.
rows.check: Proposition 5 is a worst-case lower bound for ridge-trained random feature models with frozen first-layer weights. It does not measure the width effect for fully trained networks in V2. Retain only as a theoretical comparator outside the listed versions.
